newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian UDF wins big election majority - official.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian UDF wins big election majority - official.

text.p: Bulgaria's Union of Democratic Forces, which has pledged to carry out belated free market reforms, won 52.26 percent in Saturday's election, official results showed on Wednesday.
The national electoral commission said the UDF and its coalition allies would have 137 seats in the 240-seat parliament, compared to 58 for the former ruling Socialists, who won 22.07 percent.
"Bulgaria has made an irrevocable choice in favour of reform and democracy, in favour of Europe," President Petar Stoyanov said in Strasbourg.
Stoyanov's election last November marked the start of a break with the ex-communist Socialists, who have controlled most of the nine governments since the end of one-party rule.

The UDF is expected to meet on Thursday to nominate party leader Ivan Kostov as prime minister, but formation of a new government may have to wait until after next week's four-day holiday for Eastern Orthodox Easter.
Of three smaller parties also entering parliament, the Union for National Salvation, a coalition dominated by ethnic Turks and monarchists, will have 19 seats.
The Euroleft, which includes many Socialist dissidents, will have 14, and the populist Bulgarian Business Bloc 12.
The new parliament is expected to hold its first session on May 5. The UDF wants all parties to agree on a declaration of principles for bringing the country out of its economic crisis.

Critics fear that linking urgent IMF-prescribed reforms to issues such as NATO membership and opening of secret police files may slow down the process, though all parties gave the UDF programme broad support on Tuesday.

The lev currency firmed to near 1,500 per dollar on Wednesday, up from 1,520-1,525 at Tuesday's close, as investors opting for high-yield government securities sold dollars. On the secondary debt market, profit-taking shaved Monday's gains.

The UDF's priorities are carrying out reforms agreed with the International Monetary Fund, fighting organised crime and corruption, opening secret police files on public figures, and bringing Bulgaria into the European Union and NATO.
The UDF has no constitutional need for other parties' support but wants a wide consensus for remedies that promise to be as painful as the disease.

The coalition won its strongest backing from the small Euroleft movement, which is expected to play a major role in the new parliament due to its good political relations with both the UDF and its former Socialist associates.

Under a $657 million reform and funding deal sealed by the IMF and an interim cabinet, Bulgaria pledged to introduce a currency board fixed exchange rate mechanism in June, speed up privatisation, and free prices and trade rules.
Under the currency board system, the amount of levs in circulation must be matched precisely by the amount of foreign exchange reserves.

Interim Prime Minister Stefan Sofianski said recently that the lev would be pegged at a rate slightly lower than the current one. The IMF envisages an average lev rate for this year of 2,000 to the dollar.
Mass protests ousted the Socialists in February, but not before a month of unrest had further held up reforms already delayed in the seven years since the end of one-party rule.

A caretaker cabinet has started the stabilisation process, bringing down monthly inflation to 12 percent in March from 243 percent in February and stabilising the lev from an all-time low of 3,000 per dollar in February.
